newsitem.title: CHINA: HK awaits constitutional ruling, reshuffles cabinet.
newsitem.headline: HK awaits constitutional ruling, reshuffles cabinet.

text.p: Hong Kong reshuffled its government for the first time under Chinese rule on Monday as it awaited a court ruling that may trigger a constitutional crisis.
The widely expected reshuffle, for which Beijing's approval had to be obtained, entailed no dramatic changes. "It's more of a sideways shuffle," a political analyst said.
Chief Executive Tung Chee-hwa made four ministerial-level changes involving the heads of the constitutional affairs, home affairs and transport branches, and a think tank.

On Tuesday Hong Kong's appeal court is set to rule on a claim, arising out of defence arguments in a criminal case, that Hong Kong entered a legal vacuum after China took over from Britain on July 1, and that its criminal laws became invalid.
If the ruling recognises this legal void, it may plunge Hong Kong's judicial system into chaos and bring into question the legitimacy of a Provisional Legislature set up by China.
The government says it has plans to deal with all scenarios, including the worst -- nullification of the legislature, which replaced a body elected in 1995.
"We will certainly respect the decision of the court," Justice Secretary Elsie Leung told reporters.
"If it turns out the Provisional Legislature is found to be illegal after all appeal channels have been exhausted, we will adopt the necessary contingency measures," she said.
Leung did not say what measures the government had conceived for tackling the worst-case scenario.
But legal experts said if there was a constitutional crisis, China-appointed leader Tung could turn to communist-ruled Beijing and its parliament for solutions.
Hong Kong's constitution, the Basic Law, derives authority from China's National people's Congress (NPC). The Basic Law sets the rules on forming a legislature in Hong Kong.
The leader of the popular Democratic Party, Martin Lee, slammed the government's top lawyer on Sunday for suggesting Hong Kong judges should cede their autonomy to China.
Under the treaty whereby Britain returned the bustling colony of 6.4 million people to China, Hong Kong is supposed to be virtually autonomous in all but defence and foreign affairs.

"I was sad to hear a senior government lawyer recently telling the Hong Kong courts to voluntarily give up some of their jurisdiction in deference to Beijing. I think this kind of talk is extremely bad for Hong Kong's future," Lee said.
Solicitor General Daniel Fung had argued in the landmark criminal case last week that the judges had no power to rule on the constitutional arguments. Only Beijing could rule on this, he said.
Ronald Arculli, a businessman and provisional legislator, said the appeal court might not see fit to rule on the issue.
"I would not be surprised that the court decides that it is not an appropriate case for the legality of the provisional legislative council to be pronounced upon," he told Reuters.

On other fronts, Hong Kong is settling down smoothly under Chinese rule. An opinion poll showed political confidence unshaken by the handover, and only 10 percent of people rated Hong Kong's economic prospects as bad.
Chinese and U.S. officials said the flagship of the U.S. 7th Fleet, the USS Blue Ridge, will sail in next Monday in the first port call by a foreign navy since China took over the territory.
An official at China's foreign ministry branch office here said foreign warships could continue to visit Hong Kong under Chinese rule, but Beijing's permission was needed for the calls.
Another sign of calm change came from China's garrison. A Beijing-controlled newspaper said the army would open bases to the public and hold celebrations with the local community.
